title: NASA Human Research Program: the five hazards and the risks of human spaceflight

pages.title: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight
pages.challenge_note: Basic information on the main hazards to humans on space missions, with links to detailed articles and reports.

pages.title: Risks of Human Spaceflight
pages.challenge_note: Basic information on the main risks to humans on space missions, with links to detailed articles and reports.

compound_note: The hazards can compound each other, so NASA studies their effects on the body together, on Earth in analogs and labs and on the International Space Station.

hazards.name: Space radiation
facts: Space radiation is invisible and cannot be felt; NASA calls it one of the most hazardous aspects of human spaceflight.
It comes from galactic cosmic rays and from solar storms (solar particle events and coronal mass ejections).
Effects include a higher cancer risk, damage to the central nervous system, altered cognition, reduced motor function and behavioural changes.
NASA continuously monitors space radiation and each astronaut's exposure.

hazards.name: Isolation and confinement
facts: Sleep loss, circadian desynchronization and work overload compound the effects of isolation.
Behavioural scientists use journaling to assess mental and emotional state during long isolation.
NASA's HERA analog (650 sq ft over two floors and a loft) hosts 45-day missions; CHAPEA simulates year-long Mars stays for four crew in a 1,700 sq ft habitat.

hazards.name: Distance from Earth
facts: Mars is on average about 140 million miles from Earth; a Mars mission lasts roughly three years, against a three-day trip to the Moon.
Communication delay is up to 20 minutes one way.
Medical care must be given with limited resources and poor communication, so crews need to be self-sufficient.

hazards.name: Gravity fields
facts: Weight-bearing bones lose on average 1% to 1.5% of their mineral density per month in spaceflight.
Body fluids shift toward the head, which may press on the eyes and change vision.
Without countermeasures, dehydration and calcium released from bone raise kidney-stone risk.
Going from weightlessness back into gravity can cause lightheadedness and fainting; on Mars crews would live at about three-eighths of Earth's gravity for up to two years.

hazards.name: Hostile/closed environments
facts: A spacecraft is both home and machine: temperature, pressure, lighting, noise and microbes all have to be managed.
Microbes that live on the body pass more easily between people in a closed habitat.
Stress hormones can rise and the immune system can change, which may increase susceptibility to allergies or illness.

coverage_levels.monitored: ASTRA measures at least one indicator for this risk and grades it.
coverage_levels.supported: ASTRA supports this risk with guidance, a routine task or a tool, without a body measurement of its own.
coverage_levels.partial: ASTRA covers part of this risk; the gap is named.

categories.name: Risks involving behavioral performance and human factors

risks.title: Risk of Altered Immune System Responses
risks.summary: Spaceflight stress can reactivate dormant viruses, causing rashes and other symptoms.

astra.how: Temperature and the daily symptom check catch fever, sore throat and skin rash early.

risks.title: Risk of Altered Sensorimotor and Vestibular Function
risks.summary: Motion sickness, coordination problems and dizziness when gravity changes.

astra.how: The reaction-time tap test and the dizziness and nausea symptoms track coordination after a gravity change.

risks.title: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations
risks.summary: Weightlessness changes circulation and heart and vessel function.

astra.how: Heart rate and blood pressure, graded for context (rest or after exercise) and against the personal baseline.

risks.title: Risk of Decompression Sickness
risks.summary: Nitrogen bubbles in tissue when moving from the spacecraft into a lower-pressure spacesuit.

astra.how: On surface missions a post-EVA breathing check is scheduled after the spacewalk and graded with after-EVA ranges. Gap: ASTRA has no dedicated decompression-sickness protocol yet.

risks.title: Risk of Host-Microorganism Interactions
risks.summary: Skin and gut microbiomes change in space, possibly increasing illness risk.

astra.how: Fever and symptom reports, with hand-hygiene and keep-items-separate guidance on the immune system card.

risks.title: Risk of Hypoxia
risks.summary: Mild low tissue oxygen, a side effect of the steps that prevent decompression sickness on spacewalks.

astra.how: Blood oxygen and breathing rate, with the Breathing difficulty emergency protocol for a red-flag result.

risks.title: Risk of Inadequate Food and Nutrition
risks.summary: Insufficient or unappealing nutrition affecting crew health and performance.

astra.how: Meal intake, weekly body mass and fasting glucose.

risks.title: Risk of Injury and Compromised Performance from Spacewalks
risks.summary: Injury, cognitive fatigue and suit hazards such as decompression sickness, low oxygen and high CO2.

astra.how: An EVA go / caution / no-go status on the Overview, and on surface missions a post-EVA breathing check graded with after-EVA ranges.

risks.title: Risk of Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness
risks.summary: Losses in bone density, muscle strength and heart and vessel performance.

astra.how: Daily exercise minutes, guided exercise sessions, and heart-rate recovery ranges after a workout.

risks.title: Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)
risks.summary: Changes to eye and brain structure; NASA calls it its leading spaceflight-related health risk.

astra.how: A weekly Amsler-grid vision self-check; sudden vision change is a red flag.

risks.title: Risk of Spaceflight-Induced Bone Changes
risks.summary: Bones weaken and become more brittle, raising fracture risk.

astra.how: Loading exercise every day, and hydration to protect the kidneys from calcium released by bone.

risks.title: Risk of Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders
risks.summary: Isolation, radiation and distance from Earth may affect crew mental health.

astra.how: Daily mood faces, sleep and reaction time, compared with the astronaut's own baseline.

risks.title: Risk of Inadequate Teamwork
risks.summary: Crew selection, teamwork under isolation, and miscommunication.

astra.how: Cooperative crew goals and buddy acknowledgements instead of a leaderboard.

risks.title: Risk of Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules
risks.summary: Chronic sleep loss, heavy workloads and disrupted body clocks.

astra.how: Sleep hours every morning and a reaction-time test to see when sleep loss is slowing the crew down.

risks.title: Risk of Inadequate Systems Operations Support
risks.summary: Crews facing unexpected problems without adequate information or training.

astra.how: Step-by-step how-to for every measurement and emergency protocols that work offline, with no Earth link needed.

risks.title: Risk of Injury from Dynamic Loads

astra.how: Exercise keeps bone and muscle ready for landing and back pain is a tracked symptom. Gap: ASTRA does not model landing loads.

risks.title: Risk of Radiation-Induced Cancers
risks.summary: Higher likelihood of cancer from space radiation exposure.

astra.how: Cumulative dose against the 600 mSv career limit, and a shelter alert during a solar particle event.
